name: The Mackinac Bridge
description:
The Mackinac Bridge spans 8 kilometers across the Straits of Mackinac, connecting Michigan's lower peninsula to the Upper Peninsula, and in 2200 it is the single most strategically contested piece of infrastructure in the state. The bridge was built in 1957 to unify Michigan's two halves. It now separates them. The UP's contested status — the war between Michigan and Wisconsin over territory and resources — has turned the bridge from a transportation link into a military chokepoint, a jurisdictional boundary, and the physical manifestation of a political crisis that nobody can resolve.

The bridge itself has been reinforced, widened, and enclosed against weather — the original open-deck design could not survive Superior storms with modern traffic loads. Ferrogate Transit operates the crossing under a dual charter from Michigan state authority and federal critical infrastructure designation. Six lanes of traffic — four automated cargo, two passenger — move across the straits in conditions that include 150 km/h winds, ice loading, and the occasional Wisconsin-aligned disruption attempt. The toll is the highest per-kilometer rate on any road in the GLMZ, justified by the crossing's irreplaceability: there is no alternative route between the peninsulas that doesn't involve a 500-kilometer detour through Wisconsin, which Michigan will not permit and Wisconsin will not facilitate.

The bridge's southern approach is controlled by a Ferrogate waystation complex. The northern approach is controlled by a joint Michigan-federal military installation that serves as the de facto entry checkpoint for the contested UP. Every vehicle, every passenger, and every cargo container crossing north is scanned, assessed, and logged by systems that report to Michigan state intelligence, federal military command, and Ferrogate's traffic management simultaneously. The bridge is the UP's umbilical cord to the lower peninsula — the supply line, the communication link, and the escape route. Cutting it would isolate 300,000 people in contested territory with no reliable alternative connection. Both sides of the UP war understand this. The bridge is defended like what it is: the only thing holding Michigan together.

sights: The bridge spanning the Straits — 8 kilometers of enclosed highway suspended above grey-green water, lit by navigation arrays
The northern approach military installation — concrete, steel, and the architecture of controlled access
The Straits below, churning with Lake Michigan and Lake Huron's currents meeting — visible through the bridge's lower observation panels
Ghostbridge Island visible 5 kilometers to the east — the analog anomaly, watching the hypermodern crossing from its disconnected shore
Automated cargo convoys crossing in formation — the UP's supply line made visible as a procession of identical vehicles
sounds: Wind — the bridge is 60 meters above the water, and the Straits funnel weather into a permanent gale
Structural stress sounds — the bridge groans, creaks, and flexes, and the sounds are monitored by sensors that detect danger before humans can
Military checkpoint operations at the northern approach — automated processing, authorization announcements, the controlled tempo of access
The water below — audible from the bridge deck on calm days, a reminder of the distance between the vehicle and the surface
smells: Strait air — the meeting point of Lake Michigan and Lake Huron, carrying the mineral signatures of both
Enclosed bridge atmosphere — filtered, recycled, and carrying the faint ozone of the scanning systems
Military installation fuel and equipment at the northern approach — the smell of preparedness
atmosphere.feel: Crossing the Mackinac Bridge is an act of commitment. You are leaving one jurisdiction, one economic reality, one set of rules, and entering another. The bridge takes 8 minutes at highway speed, and in those 8 minutes you are suspended between two worlds — literally, above the water, between the peninsulas, in transit between the stable south and the contested north. The bridge does not feel safe. The bridge feels necessary.

demographics: No permanent residential population on the bridge itself. The waystation complexes at each approach house approximately 2,000 personnel — Ferrogate operators, military staff, security contractors, and the service workers who support them. Transient crossing population averages 15,000 per day, with significant variation based on UP conditions, weather, and the current state of the territorial dispute.
economy: Toll revenue (Ferrogate Transit) and military logistics. The bridge generates approximately 850 million Q annually in toll revenue, making it one of the most profitable single pieces of infrastructure in the GLMZ. The military installation at the northern approach is federally funded. The economics are simple: the bridge is irreplaceable, so it charges accordingly.
power_structure: Ferrogate Transit operating charter, Michigan state authority, and federal military designation — three jurisdictions layered on 8 kilometers of bridge deck. Ferrogate handles traffic and maintenance. Michigan handles civil authority. The military handles security. Conflicts between the three are resolved by whoever has the most immediate operational necessity, which is usually the military.
dangers: Weather — Straits storms can close the bridge, isolating the UP from its supply line
Structural vulnerability — the bridge is reinforced but irreplaceable, and its destruction would be catastrophic for 300,000 UP residents
Military escalation — the northern checkpoint's rules of engagement are classified, and crossing incidents are adjudicated by military tribunal
Wisconsin-aligned disruption attempts — the bridge has been targeted multiple times, and the attempts are growing more sophisticated
Toll economics as population control — Ferrogate's pricing determines who can afford to cross, which determines who can access the UP
opportunities: Bridge crossing intelligence — the checkpoint data reveals everything about UP supply, personnel movement, and military readiness
Ferrogate transit contracts — the bridge needs maintenance, and the contracts are valuable
The straits beneath the bridge — unmonitored water routes between the lakes that bypass the checkpoint entirely
Military liaison — the bridge's federal designation creates opportunities for operators with the right clearances
story_hooks: Structural sensors on the bridge have detected anomalies that don't match weather stress or traffic loading — something is affecting the bridge's integrity from below
A Wisconsin-aligned team has developed a plan to close the bridge for 30 days — long enough to starve the UP of supplies and force Michigan to the negotiating table
Ferrogate Transit has been selectively allowing unscanned cargo across the bridge on a schedule that correlates with Wisconsin intelligence deliveries — the bridge operator is playing both sides

Military convoys and personnel moving to UP deployments
Civilian travelers crossing between the peninsulas
Ferrogate Transit operators and bridge maintenance crews
